indications.text: 1 INDICATIONS AND USAGE ONSWIK™ is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. ONSWIK™ is a long-acting insulin analog indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. ( 1 ) Limitations of Use: Not recommended for use in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus due to increased risk of severe hypoglycemia ( 1 ) Limitations of Use ONSWIK is not recommended for use in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus due to increased risk of severe hypoglycemia. [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 )] .

dosage.text: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION See Full Prescribing Information for general dosing and important administration instructions. ( 2.1 , 2.2 ) Administer once weekly on the same day each week. The scheduled injection day may be changed, provided 4 days have elapsed since the last dose. Once the injection day is changed, continue administering ONSWIK on the new chosen day. ( 2.1 ) Individualize and adjust the dosage based on metabolic needs, glucose monitoring results and glycemic control goal. ( 2.1 ) Inject subcutaneously into the abdomen, upper arm, thigh, or buttocks. ( 2.2 ) Rotate injection sites to reduce risk of lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis. ( 2.2 ) May administer alone or in any combination with oral and injectable antidiabetic medicines and bolus insulin. ( 2.2 ) See Full Prescribing Information for recommended starting dosage in insulin naïve patients and patients already on a daily basal insulin. ( 2.3 , 2.4 ) 2.1 General Dosing Instructions ONSWIK is available as a single-patient-use prefilled pen (KwikPen) in 2 concentrations (U-500 and U-1,000). The U-500 KwikPen delivers doses in 5-unit increments and can deliver up to 400 units in a single injection. The U-1,000 KwikPen delivers doses in 10-unit increments and can deliver up to 800 units in a single injection. Administer ONSWIK by subcutaneous injection once weekly on the same day each week. If necessary, the scheduled injection day may be changed, provided at least 4 days have elapsed since the last dose. Once the injection day is changed, continue administering ONSWIK on the new chosen day. Do not repeat administration of the one-time starting dose [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.6 ), Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Individualize and adjust the dosage of ONSWIK based on metabolic needs, glucose monitoring results and glycemic control goal. If glycemic control does not improve despite adherence to diet, medication adherence, and escalating dosages of ONSWIK, consider switching to another insulin product [see Immunogenicity ( 12.6 )] . The potency of insulin analogs, including ONSWIK, is expressed in units. One ( 1 ) unit of ONSWIK corresponds to 1 international unit of human insulin. Consider the long half-life of ONSWIK when adjusting the dosage. When the dosage is adjusted, initial changes in fasting blood glucose (FBG) are expected within 1 to 2 weeks, with the full treatment effect of the dosage adjustment occurring in approximately 4 weeks [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 , 12.3 )] . Dosage adjustment is not recommended during acute illness nor when patients make short-term changes in their physical activity level or usual diet. In these situations, consider other applicable adjustments, e.g., glucose intake or changes to other glucose lowering medication [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 , 12.3 )] . 2.2 Important Administration Instructions Always check insulin labels before administration [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Inspect ONSWIK visually before use. Only use ONSWIK if the solution is clear and colorless to yellow with no visible particles. Prior to initiation, train patients and their caregiver(s) on how to select their weekly ONSWIK dosage. Instruct patients to visually verify the dialed units on the dose window of the ONSWIK KwikPen before each injection to avoid dosing errors, including underdosage and overdosage, that may lead to hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, respectively. Inject ONSWIK subcutaneously into the abdomen, upper arm, thigh, or buttocks. Rotate injection sites within the same region from one injection to the next to reduce the risk of lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis. Do not inject into areas of lipodystrophy or localized cutaneous amyloidosis [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 ), Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )] . During changes to a patient's insulin regimen, increase the frequency of glucose monitoring [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 )] . Use ONSWIK prefilled pen products with caution in patients with visual impairment who may rely on audible clicks to dial their dose. ONSWIK may be administered alone or in any combination with oral and injectable antidiabetic medicines and rapid-acting or short-acting insulin products. Do not administer ONSWIK intramuscularly, intravenously or in an insulin pump. Do not dilute or mix ONSWIK with any insulin product or other solutions. Do not transfer ONSWIK from the prefilled pen to a syringe for administration [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . 2.3 Recommended Dosage in Insulin Naïve Patients There are two dosing options for insulin naïve patients: a fixed-dosage titration and a flexible-dosage titration. Fixed-Dosage Titration The recommended starting dosage is 100 units injected subcutaneously once weekly on the same day each week. After a minimum of 4 weeks, titrate the dosage based on the patient's metabolic needs, glucose monitoring results and glycemic goal according to Table 1 . Table 1: Fixed-Dosage Titration Dosing Dosage (units) once weekly Recommended starting dosage 100 After a minimum of 4 weeks on a stable dose, if the fasting glycemic goal has not been reached and the FBG is above 130 mg/dL, titrate sequentially to the next higher dose shown on the right. If the patient experiences hypoglycemia within the prior week, withhold further dosage increases until the cause has been addressed and hypoglycemia has resolved. 150 250 400 If the FBG is below 130 mg/dL and the fasting glycemic goal has not been reached, titrate the dosage by 20 to 40 units per week as necessary. If a dosage greater than 400 units once weekly is required to reach glycemic goal, titrate the dosage by 20 to 40 units per week as necessary. Flexible-Dosage Titration See Table 2 for dosage and important considerations for the flexible-dosage titration. Table 2: Flexible-Dosage Titration Week Dosage (units) Important Considerations First week 300 The 300-unit One-Time Starting Dose is only administered during the first week. Second week 100 Do not repeat the 300-unit One-Time Starting Dose. Third and subsequent weeks Adjust the ONSWIK dosage by 20 units to 40 units per week. Titrate the dosage as necessary based on the patient's fasting glycemic goal. 2.4 Switching from Once- or Twice-Daily Basal Insulin to ONSWIK Administer the first dose of ONSWIK on the day after the last dose of once- or twice-daily basal insulin. Close glucose monitoring is recommended during the switch and until the dosage and glycemic control are stable. Doses and timing of concurrent mealtime insulin products or other concomitant antidiabetic medications may require adjustments. See Table 3 for dosage calculations and important considerations when switching patients from once- or twice-daily basal insulin to ONSWIK. Table 3: Switching From Once- or Twice-Daily Basal Insulin to ONSWIK a Round calculated doses to the nearest 5 units for the U-500 KwikPen and 10 units for the U-1,000 KwikPen. b For patients switching from once-daily insulin glargine 300 units/mL or twice-daily NPH insulin to ONSWIK, use 80% of the total daily insulin glargine or NPH insulin dosage when calculating ONSWIK dosages. Weekly Dosage Dosage Calculation (units) a Important Considerations First week One-Time Starting Dose: Multiply the total daily basal b insulin dosage by 7, then multiply by 3. The One - Time Starting Dose is only administered during the first week. For patients who have FBG values less than or equal to 120 mg/dL on daily basal insulin: Consider omitting the One-Time Starting Dose. Instead, the first week dose is the total daily basal b insulin dosage multiplied by 7 If the One-Time Starting Dose is omitted: Transient hyperglycemia may occur and last 4 to 6 weeks. Second week Multiply the previous total daily basal b insulin dosage by 7 Do not repeat the One-Time Starting Dose. Third and subsequent weeks Adjust the ONSWIK dosage by 20 units to 40 units per week, as necessary based on the fasting glycemic goal. If the One-Time Starting Dose was omitted: Do not adjust the weekly dosage of ONSWIK until FBG levels have stabilized. If the FBG level is stable and remains above the goal, the dosage may be adjusted, as necessary based on the patient's fasting glycemic goal. 2.5 Recommendations Regarding Missed Dose If a dose is missed: Administer the missed dose as soon as possible within 4 days of the missed dose then maintain the regular weekly dosing schedule. If more than 4 days have passed there are two options. Patients can skip the missed dose and administer the usual dose on the regularly scheduled day. Alternatively, patients can administer the missed dose then resume the once-weekly dosing schedule, one week from the day the missed dose was administered. Increase blood glucose monitoring with missed dosage. 2.6 Management of Accidental Extra Dose(s) If the one-time starting dose is accidentally administered more than once (for example, if the one-time starting dose is administered for 2 consecutive weeks), skip the next week's dose. If the weekly dosage is administered more than once in the same week, skip the next week's dose. Monitor glucose levels more frequently and assess for repeated or severe hypoglycemia.

contraindications.text: 4 CONTRAINDICATIONS ONSWIK is contraindicated: during episodes of hypoglycemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )]. in patients with hypersensitivity to insulin efsitora alfa-gobe or any of the excipients in ONSWIK. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have occurred with insulin and insulin analogs [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.5 )] . warnings.text: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Hypoglycemia Due to Medication Errors and Accidental Overdose: Accidental mix-ups between insulin products can occur. Advise patients to always check the product label before each injection to confirm they are using ONSWIK and not another insulin or injectable antidiabetic medicine. Do not transfer ONSWIK into a syringe as overdosage and severe hypoglycemia can result. Do not repeat the one-time starting dose after the first injection. ( 5.1 ) Hypoglycemia: May be life-threatening. Increase frequency of glucose monitoring with changes to insulin dosage, co-administered glucose-lowering medications, meal pattern, physical activity, and in patients with renal impairment or hepatic impairment or hypoglycemia unawareness. ( 5.3 ) Hyperglycemia or Hypoglycemia with changes in insulin regimen: Make changes to a patient's insulin regimen (e.g., insulin strength, manufacturer, type, injection site or method of administration) under close medical supervision with increased frequency of glucose monitoring. ( 5.4 ) Hypersensitivity Reactions: Severe, life-threatening, generalized allergy, including anaphylaxis, can occur. Discontinue ONSWIK, monitor and treat if indicated. ( 5.5 ) Hypokalemia: May be life-threatening. Monitor potassium levels in patients at risk for hypokalemia and treat if indicated. ( 5.6 ) Never share ONSWIK between patients, even if the needle is changed. ( 5.7 ) Fluid Retention and Heart Failure with Concomitant Use of PPAR-Gamma Agonists: Observe for signs and symptoms of heart failure; consider dosage reduction or discontinuation of the PPAR-gamma agonist if heart failure occurs. ( 5.8 ) 5.1 Hypoglycemia Due to Medication Errors and Accidental Overdose Serious hypoglycemia requiring hospitalization has occurred due to accidental mix-ups between once-weekly insulin products and other insulin products or once-weekly injectable antidiabetic medicines, incorrect dose selection, and dosing frequency errors. To avoid dosing errors when switching from daily basal insulin to ONSWIK, follow the dosage recommendations in the Dosage and Administration Section ( 2.4 ). Administer ONSWIK once weekly only. Do not repeat administration of the one-time starting dose. Advise patients to always check the product label before each injection to confirm they are using ONSWIK and not another insulin or injectable antidiabetic medicine. Prior to initiation, train patients and their caregiver(s) on how to select their weekly ONSWIK dosage. Advise patients using other injectable medications for glycemic control that the dosage selection of ONSWIK differs. Instruct patients to visually verify the dialed units on the dose window of the ONSWIK KwikPen before each injection to avoid dosing errors. Patients should not dial the maximum single dose (400 units for the U-500 KwikPen or 800 units for the U-1,000 KwikPen) of ONSWIK unless this is the prescribed dose Patients should not use a syringe to remove ONSWIK from the ONSWIK KwikPen. The markings on the syringe will not measure the dose correctly and this can result in overdosage and severe hypoglycemia [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.2 , 2.3 , 2.4 ), Instructions for Use] . Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia, particularly during the first several weeks after initiation or dose escalation of ONSWIK. Ensure patients understand how to recognize and manage hypoglycemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )]. 5.2 Severe Hypoglycemia in Patients with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus ONSWIK is not recommended for use in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus due to increased risk of severe hypoglycemia. In a 52-week clinical trial of adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus, the incidence of Level 3 (severe) hypoglycemia was higher for patients treated with ONSWIK compared with insulin degludec (10% versus 3%). 5.3 Hypoglycemia Hypoglycemia is the most common adverse reaction associated with insulins, including ONSWIK [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )] . Severe hypoglycemia can cause seizures, may lead to unconsciousness, may be life-threatening, or cause death. Hypoglycemia can impair concentration ability and reaction time; this may place an individual and others at risk in situations where these abilities are important (e.g., driving or operating other machinery). Hypoglycemia can happen suddenly, and symptoms may differ in each individual and change over time in the same individual. Symptomatic awareness of hypoglycemia may be less pronounced in patients with longstanding diabetes, in patients with diabetic nerve disease, in patients using medications that block the sympathetic nervous system (e.g., beta-blockers) [see Drug Interactions ( 7 )] , or in patients who experience recurrent hypoglycemia. The long-acting effect of ONSWIK may delay recovery from hypoglycemia compared to shorter-acting insulins [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 , 12.3 )] . Risk Factors for Hypoglycemia The risk of hypoglycemia generally increases with intensity of glycemic control. The risk of hypoglycemia after an injection is related to the duration of action of the insulin [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 )] and, in general, is highest when the glucose lowering effect of the insulin is maximal. As with all insulins, the glucose lowering effect over time of ONSWIK may vary among different individuals or at different times in the same individual and depends on many conditions, including the area of injection as well as the injection site blood supply and temperature. Other factors that may increase the risk of hypoglycemia include changes in meal pattern (e.g., macronutrient content or timing of meals), changes in level of physical activity, or changes to co-administered medication [see Drug Interactions ( 7 ) ] . Patients with renal or hepatic impairment may be at higher risk of hypoglycemia [see Use in Specific Populations ( 8.6 , 8.7 )]. Risk Mitigation Strategies for Hypoglycemia Educate patients and caregivers to recognize and manage hypoglycemia. Self-monitoring of blood glucose plays an essential role in the prevention and management of hypoglycemia. In patients at higher risk for hypoglycemia and patients who have reduced symptomatic awareness of hypoglycemia, increased frequency of blood glucose monitoring is recommended. 5.4 Hyperglycemia or Hypoglycemia with Changes in Insulin Regimen Changes in an insulin regimen (e.g., insulin strength, manufacturer, type, injection site or method of administration) may affect glycemic control and predispose to hypoglycemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )] or hyperglycemia. Repeated insulin injections into areas of lipodystrophy or localized cutaneous amyloidosis have been reported to result in hyperglycemia; and a sudden change in the injection site (to an unaffected area) has been reported to result in hypoglycemia [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )]. The risk of hyperglycemia may be increased during the first four to six weeks of titration, especially if ONSWIK is initiated without the one-time starting dose [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.3 , 2.4 ), Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 , 12.3 )] . Make any changes to a patient's insulin regimen under close medical supervision with increased frequency of glucose monitoring. Advise patients who have repeatedly injected into areas of lipodystrophy or localized cutaneous amyloidosis to change the injection site to unaffected areas and closely monitor for hypoglycemia. Adjustments in concomitant anti-diabetic treatment may be needed [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.3 , 2.4 )]. 5.5 Hypersensitivity Reactions Severe, life-threatening, generalized allergy, including anaphylaxis, can occur with insulins, including ONSWIK [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )] . If hypersensitivity reactions occur, discontinue ONSWIK; treat per standard of care and monitor until symptoms and signs resolve. ONSWIK is contraindicated in patients who have had hypersensitivity reactions to insulin efsitora alfa-gobe or any of the excipients in ONSWIK [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . 5.6 Hypokalemia All insulins, including ONSWIK, cause a shift in potassium from the extracellular to intracellular space, possibly leading to hypokalemia. Untreated hypokalemia may cause respiratory paralysis, ventricular arrhythmia, and death. Monitor potassium levels in patients at risk for hypokalemia (e.g., patients using potassium-lowering medications, patients taking medications sensitive to serum potassium concentrations) and treat if indicated. 5.7 Never Share an ONSWIK Prefilled Pen Between Patients ONSWIK prefilled pens must never be shared between patients, even if the needle is changed. Sharing poses a risk for transmission of blood-borne pathogens. 5.8 Fluid Retention and Heart Failure with Concomitant Use of PPAR-Gamma Agonists Thiazolidinediones (TZDs), which are peroxisome proliferator activated receptor (PPAR)-gamma agonists, can cause dose-related fluid retention, when used in combination with insulin. Fluid retention may lead to or exacerbate heart failure. Patients treated with insulin, including ONSWIK and a PPAR-gamma agonist should be observed for signs and symptoms of heart failure. If heart failure develops, it should be managed according to current standards of care and discontinuation or dose reduction of the PPAR-gamma agonist must be considered.

adverse_reactions.text: 6 ADVERSE REACTIONS The following adverse reactions are described below or elsewhere in the prescribing information: Hypoglycemia Due to Medication Errors and Accidental Overdose [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Severe Hypoglycemia in Patients with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 )] . Hypoglycemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )] . Hypersensitivity Reactions [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.5 )] . Hypokalemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.6 )]. Common adverse reactions include hypoglycemia, hypersensitivity reactions, injection site reactions, lipodystrophy, pruritus, rash, edema, and weight gain. ( 6.1 ) To report SUSPECTED ADVERSE REACTIONS, contact Eli Lilly and Company at 1-800-LillyRx (1-800-545-5979) or FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or www.fda.gov/medwatch. 6.1 Clinical Trials Experience Because clinical trials are conducted under widely varying conditions, adverse reaction rates observed in the clinical trials of a drug cannot be directly compared to rates in the clinical trials of another drug and may not reflect the rates observed in clinical practice. The safety of ONSWIK was evaluated in four clinical trials involving 1,883 adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus exposed to ONSWIK, with a mean exposure duration of 372 days [see Clinical Studies ( 14 )] . The mean age was 59 years, the mean duration of diabetes was 13 years, 55% were male, 63% were White, 21% were Asian, 10% were American Indian or Alaska Native, 5% were Black or African American, and 45% were Hispanic. The mean BMI was 31 kg/m 2 and the mean HbA1c at baseline was 8.1%. Common Adverse Reactions Hypoglycemia Hypoglycemia is the most common adverse reaction in patients using insulin, including ONSWIK. The frequency of reported hypoglycemia depends on the definition of hypoglycemia used, diabetes type, insulin dose, intensity of glucose control, background therapies, and other intrinsic and extrinsic patient factors. For these reasons, comparing the frequency of hypoglycemia in clinical trials for ONSWIK with the frequency of hypoglycemia for other products may be misleading and may not be representative of hypoglycemia frequencies that occur in clinical practice. In clinical trials [see Clinical Studies ( 14 )], events of severe hypoglycemia (level 3) were defined as an episode associated with severe cognitive impairment requiring external assistance for recovery. Hypoglycemia episodes with a glucose level below 54 mg/dL with or without associated symptoms (level 2 hypoglycemia) were also assessed in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. In clinical trials in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, the proportions of adults treated with ONSWIK who experienced at least one episode of level 3 and/or level 2 hypoglycemia in clinical trials are shown in Table 4 . Trial 1 Insulin Naïve Adults on Fixed-Dosage Titration (0-52 weeks) N=397 Trial 2 Insulin Naïve Adults on Flexible-Dosage Titration (0-52 weeks) N=466 Trial 3 Adults Previously Treated with Daily Basal Insulin (0-78 weeks) N=655 Trial 4 Adults Previously Treated with Daily Basal and Mealtime Insulin (0-26 weeks) N=365 Level 3 hypoglycemia a 0.3 0 0.9 1.4 Level 3 and/or Level 2 hypoglycemia b 25.9 27.9 40.9 55.6 Insulin Initiation and Intensification of Glucose Control Intensification or rapid improvement in glucose control has been associated with a transitory, reversible ophthalmologic refraction disorder, worsening of diabetic retinopathy, and acute painful peripheral neuropathy. However, long-term glycemic control decreases the risk of diabetic retinopathy and neuropathy. Allergic Reactions Severe, life-threatening, generalized allergy, including anaphylaxis, generalized skin reactions, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, and shock may occur with any insulin, including ONSWIK. Hypersensitivity reactions were reported in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with ONSWIK: contact dermatitis (0.7%), rash (0.7%), dermatitis (0.7%), hypersensitivity (0.6%), pruritus (0.6%), eczema (0.6%) and allergic rhinitis (0.5%). Lipodystrophy Long-term use of insulin, including ONSWIK, can cause lipodystrophy at the site of repeated insulin injections. Lipodystrophy includes lipohypertrophy (thickening of adipose tissue) and lipoatrophy (thinning of adipose tissue) and may affect insulin absorption [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.2 )]. Lipodystrophy was reported in 0.3% of adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with ONSWIK. Injection Site Reactions Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus taking ONSWIK have experienced redness, hardening, pain, bruising, swelling or itching at the site of ONSWIK injection. Injection site reactions occurred in 1.4% of adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with ONSWIK. No patients treated with ONSWIK in the clinical trials discontinued ONSWIK due to injection site-related reactions. Weight Gain Weight gain can occur with insulin therapy, including ONSWIK, and has been attributed to the anabolic effects of insulin and the decrease in glucosuria. Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with ONSWIK with or without mealtime insulin therapy gained an average of 1.9 to 3.2 kg after 26 weeks of treatment. Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with ONSWIK without mealtime insulin therapy gained an average of 2.1 to 3.9 kg after 52 weeks of treatment. Peripheral Edema ONSWIK may cause sodium retention and edema. Peripheral edema occurred in 1.6% of adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with ONSWIK.

specific_populations.text: 8 USE IN SPECIFIC POPULATIONS Pregnancy: Use during pregnancy is not recommended. ( 8.1 ) Lactation: Use during breastfeeding or lactation is not recommended. ( 8.2 ) 8.1 Pregnancy Risk Summary The use of ONSWIK during pregnancy is not recommended. Available data with ONSWIK use in pregnant women are insufficient to evaluate for a drug-related risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. There are risks to the mother and fetus associated with poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy ( see Clinical Considerations ). Based on animal reproduction studies, there may be risks to the fetus from exposure to ONSWIK during pregnancy. In pregnant rats or rabbits administered insulin efsitora alfa-gobe during organogenesis, early embryonic deaths, and fetal abnormalities occurred at clinically relevant exposures at the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) of 1,400 units /week and were associated with hypoglycemia in maternal non-diabetic animals. Hypoglycemia-related mortality occurred in rats during pregnancy and following birth, and pup mortality occurred during the lactation period, which correlated with plasma exposure levels of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe and severe hypoglycemia in pups. Human IgG is known to cross the placental barrier via FcRn transfer; therefore, insulin efsitora alfa-gobe may be transmitted from the mother to the developing fetus in late pregnancy. The estimated background risk of major birth defects is 6% to 10% in women with pre - gestational diabetes with a HbA1c>7% and has been reported to be as high as 20% to 25% in women with a HbA1c >10%. The estimated background risk of miscarriage for the indicated population is unknown. In the U.S. general population, the estimated background risk of major birth defects and miscarriage in clinically recognized pregnancies is 2% to 4% and 15% to 20%, respectively. Clinical Considerations Disease-associated Maternal and/or Embryo-Fetal Risk Poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy increases the maternal risk for diabetic ketoacidosis, pre - eclampsia, spontaneous abortions, preterm delivery, and delivery complications. Poorly controlled diabetes increases the fetal risk for major birth defects, stillbirth, and macrosomia related morbidity. Data Animal Data In pregnant rats, insulin efsitora alfa-gobe did not cause adverse effects on embryo-fetal development when given subcutaneously during organogenesis at doses of 22 and 75 units/kg/week, which were up to 0.2-fold the MRHD, based on AUC. However, increased post-implantation loss secondary to maternal hypoglycemia was observed when rats were given 75 units/kg/week insulin efsitora alfa-gobe prior to and during mating and through early gestation (Gestation Day 6) at clinically relevant exposures. In pregnant rabbits given subcutaneous doses during organogenesis of 6 and 22 units/kg/week insulin efsitora alfa-gobe weekly, which were up to 0.1-fold the MRHD, post-implantation losses and fetal skeletal/visceral abnormalities were observed at clinically relevant exposures, which were secondary to maternal hypoglycemia. In a pre- and postnatal developmental study in rats where insulin efsitora alfa-gobe was given subcutaneously from implantation through the end of lactation (Gestation Day 6 through Lactation Day 20) at doses of 22 and 75 units/kg/week, which were up to 0.6-fold the MRHD, hypoglycemia-related maternal mortality during or following birth and pup mortality during the lactation period occurred at clinically relevant exposures. There was plasma exposure of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe and severe hypoglycemia in pups, which is likely due to FcRn-mediated transfer of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe. 8.2 Lactation Risk Summary The use of ONSWIK during breastfeeding or lactation is not recommended. There are no data on the presence of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe in animal or human milk, the effects on the breastfed infant, or the effects on milk production. Based on plasma exposure levels of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe in rat pups, there is indirect evidence of presence of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe in the milk. 8.4 Pediatric Use Safety and effectiveness of ONSWIK have not been established in pediatric patients. ONSWIK is not recommended for use in pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus due to increased risk of severe hypoglycemia [ see Indications and Usage ( 1 ) and Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 ) ]. 8.5 Geriatric Use In clinical trials, 30% (561/1,883) of ONSWIK - treated patients were 65 years of age or older, and 5% (85/1,883) of ONSWIK - treated patients were 75 years of age or older at baseline. No overall differences in safety or effectiveness of ONSWIK have been observed between patients 65 years of age and older and younger adult patients. Greater caution should be exercised when ONSWIK is administered to geriatric patients since greater sensitivity of some older individuals to the effects of ONSWIK cannot be ruled out. The initial dosing, dose increments, and maintenance dosage should be conservative to avoid hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia may be more difficult to recognize in the elderly. More frequent glucose monitoring is recommended, and the insulin dose is to be adjusted on an individual basis. 8.6 Renal Impairment No clinically relevant differences in the pharmacokinetics of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe were observed across the different renal impairment subgroups [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )] . Additional dose adjustment should not be necessary for patients with renal impairment. However, as with all insulin products, glucose monitoring should be intensified and the ONSWIK dosage adjusted on an individual basis in patients with renal impairment. 8.7 Hepatic Impairment No difference in the pharmacokinetics of ONSWIK was identified comparing healthy subjects and subjects with hepatic impairment [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )] . Additional dose adjustment should not be necessary for patients with hepatic impairment. However, as with all insulin products, glucose monitoring should be intensified and the ONSWIK dosage adjusted on an individual basis in patients with hepatic impairment.

mechanism.text: 12.1 Mechanism of Action The primary activity of ONSWIK is the regulation of glucose metabolism. Insulin and its analogs lower blood glucose by stimulating peripheral glucose uptake, especially by skeletal muscle and fat, and by inhibiting hepatic glucose production. Insulin also inhibits lipolysis and proteolysis and enhances protein synthesis. The protracted time-action profile of ONSWIK results from reduced renal clearance due to its relatively large molecular size, inhibition of degradation due to binding at the neonatal Fc receptor, and reduced affinity relative to human insulin for the insulin receptor, which decreases receptor-mediated clearance. Once insulin efsitora alfa-gobe is engaged with the insulin receptor, it results in the same pharmacological effects as human insulin.

pharmacokinetics.text: 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption Absorption of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe was evaluated in healthy subjects and adults with diabetes. Steady-state pharmacokinetics (PK) was achieved between the eighth and tenth weeks after initiating ONSWIK without a one-time starting dose and between the fourth and sixth weeks after initiating ONSWIK with a one-time starting dose of 3 times the weekly dose [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.3 , 2.4 )] . At steady-state, time to maximum insulin efsitora alfa-gobe concentration was achieved at 2.5 days post dose (Tmax). ONSWIK has a peak-to-trough ratio of 1.16 and the week-to-week variability (CV%) in total exposure of ONSWIK was 5%. The absolute bioavailability of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe after subcutaneous administration into the abdomen, was approximately 86%. Injection site (abdomen, upper arm, or thigh) did not influence the absorption or exposure of ONSWIK. Total insulin efsitora alfa-gobe exposure and maximum insulin efsitora alfa-gobe concentration increased proportionally with increasing subcutaneous doses of ONSWIK within the therapeutic dose range. No dose conversion is required if transferring a patient between the U-500 and U-1,000 strengths when each is administered at the same units/kg dose. Distribution Following a 100-unit subcutaneous bolus injection of ONSWIK, the geometric mean (CV%) volume of distribution of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe (Vd) was 13 L (24%). Elimination Following a 100-unit subcutaneous bolus injection of ONSWIK, the geometric mean (CV%) clearance of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe (CL) was 0.02 L/h (24%). The geometric mean (CV%) elimination half-life at steady-state is approximately 17 days (26%), independent of dose. Specific Populations No clinically significant differences in the pharmacokinetics of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe were observed based on age (18 to 88 years), sex (56% male and 44% female), race (67% White, 4.7% Black, 8.4% American Indian or Alaska Native, and 19% Asian), renal function (based on race-free CKD-EPI 2021 category) or based on alanine aminotransferase (ALT 5 to 398 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST 5 to 325 U/L). The effect of hemodialysis with kidney failure or severe hepatic impairment on the pharmacokinetics of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe is unknown. Insulin efsitora alfa-gobe exposure decreased with increasing body weight (43 to 157 kg), but these effects are mitigated by the recommended dosing based on glycemic control.
